Protect yourself, Duryodhana; the self is the vessel of all. When a vessel is broken, dear one, what it contains goes in all directions.
mahabharata:9:3.42	One who is declining should seek peace, one who is equal war, one who is rising conquest; this is Brihaspati's policy.
mahabharata:9:3.43	We, declined from the Pandavas in our strength and power, are in that position; I think peace with the Pandavas is fitting for you here, lord.
mahabharata:9:3.44	He who does not know what is good and slights what is good soon falls from his kingdom and does not obtain good.
mahabharata:9:3.45	If by bowing to the king we could get the kingdom, that would be good; but, king, we should not go to ruin through folly.
mahabharata:9:3.46	By the word of Vichitravirya's son (Dhritarashtra) and by Govinda's word, the compassionate Yudhishthira would reinstate you in the kingdom.
mahabharata:9:3.47	Whatever Hrishikesha says to the unconquered king, Arjuna and Bhimasena would do without doubt.
mahabharata:9:3.48	Krishna will not transgress the word of the Kaurava Dhritarashtra, I think, nor will the Pandava transgress Krishna's.
mahabharata:9:3.49	I think this fitting: no war between you and the Parthas. I do not say this from wretchedness or to protect my life; I say it for your good, king; when you are dying you will remember it.
The aged Kripa Sharadvata, lamenting thus, sighed long and hot, grieved and fell into stupor.
Then, after reflecting a moment, the great-minded Dhritarashtra's son, tormentor of foes, spoke these words to Kripa Sharadvata:

Whatever a friend should say, all that I have been told, and you have done all, fighting giving up life.
mahabharata:9:4.4	Plunging into the divisions and fighting with the Pandavas, great chariot-warriors of exceeding splendour, the world has watched you.
mahabharata:9:4.5	What you, as a friend, should say, you have told me; yet none of it pleases me, as medicine does not please one who wishes to die.
mahabharata:9:4.6	Excellent, wholesome words with reason and cause, mighty-armed one, are spoken, but they do not please me, best of Brahmanas.
mahabharata:9:4.7	We deprived him of his kingdom; how would he trust us? At dice we conquered the king of great wealth; how would he believe my words again?
mahabharata:9:4.8	Likewise Krishna, devoted to Partha's good, came as an envoy, and Hrishikesha was deceived and that act opposed; how, Brahmana, will he accept my word?
mahabharata:9:4.9	What Krishna (Draupadi) lamented when she was brought in the midst of the assembly, Krishna (the Lord) cannot forgive that, nor the seizing of the kingdom.
mahabharata:9:4.11	Hearing that his sister's son was slain, Keshava sleeps in pain; we have offended him; how would he forgive me?
mahabharata:9:4.12	Arjuna finds no peace after Abhimanyu's destruction; how would he strive for my good, if asked?
mahabharata:9:4.13	The middle Pandava, sharp, mighty Bhimasena, has taken a fierce vow; he would break but not bend.
mahabharata:9:4.14	Both twins have swords bound and armour bound, both heroes have made enmity, like Yama himself.
mahabharata:9:4.15	Dhrishtadyumna and Shikhandin have made enmity with me; how would they, best of Brahmanas, strive for my good?
mahabharata:9:4.16	What Duhshasana did to Krishna in one garment, in her season, tormented in the midst of the assembly in the sight of all the world—
mahabharata:9:4.17	the Pandavas, remembering her unclothed and wretched even now, scorchers of foes, cannot be held back from battle.
mahabharata:9:4.18	And Draupadi Krishna, grieved for my destruction, practised fierce austerity for the success of her husbands, always sleeping on the bare ground until vengeance be done.
mahabharata:9:4.19	Casting aside pride and arrogance, Vasudeva's sister, as one to look after, always serves Krishna.
mahabharata:9:4.20	Thus all this is swollen and never abates; with Abhimanyu's destruction, how could I make peace?
mahabharata:9:4.21	How, having enjoyed this earth girdled by the sea, could I enjoy a small kingdom by the Pandavas' grace?
mahabharata:9:4.22	Having shone over kings like the blazing sun, how could I afterwards follow Yudhishthira like a slave?
mahabharata:9:4.23	How, having enjoyed pleasures myself and given abundant gifts, shall I live a wretched life with the wretched?
mahabharata:9:4.24	I do not find fault with your word, spoken kindly and wholesomely; but I do not think peace timely in any way.
mahabharata:9:4.25	I see good policy in good fighting, scorcher of foes; this is not the time to become weak, it is the time to fight.
mahabharata:9:4.26	I have sacrificed with many sacrifices, given gifts to Brahmanas, learned the Vedas in order, and stand on the heads of my foes.
mahabharata:9:4.27	Servants have been well maintained, the afflicted raised up, enemy countries gone through, my own realm protected.
mahabharata:9:4.28	Many pleasures enjoyed, the three aims of life pursued by me, I have discharged my debt to my fathers and to kshatriya duty both.
mahabharata:9:4.29	There is no sure happiness here; whence kingdom, whence fame? Fame is to be made here, and that by war, not otherwise.
mahabharata:9:4.30	That a kshatriya should die at home is condemned; it is a very great unrighteousness to die on a bed at home.
mahabharata:9:4.31	The man who gives up his body in the forest or in battle, having performed great sacrifices, attains greatness.
mahabharata:9:4.32	One who dies wretched, lamenting, afflicted, overrun by old age, among weeping kinsmen, is no man.
mahabharata:9:4.33	Having given up many pleasures, may I now go by good fighting to the supreme goal of those who attain the world of the good.
mahabharata:9:4.34	Of the brave, of noble conduct, never turning back in battles, wise, true to their word, all performers of sacrifices,
mahabharata:9:4.35	who have attained the final bath by weapons, there is surely a dwelling in heaven; the bright hosts of apsarases surely look on them with joy.
mahabharata:9:4.36	The fathers surely see them honoured in Shakra's assembly, surrounded by apsarases and rejoicing in heaven.
mahabharata:9:4.37	The path travelled by immortals and by brave men who never turned back—may we too ascend that road, meeting them.
mahabharata:9:4.38	With the aged Grandsire, with the wise preceptor, with Jayadratha, Karna and Duhshasana,
mahabharata:9:4.39	striving for me here, brave lords of men are slain, lying on the earth with limbs smeared with blood, wounded by arrows.
mahabharata:9:4.40	Brave men, knowers of the finest weapons, performers of sacrifices as prescribed, giving up life properly, stand in Indra's mansions.
mahabharata:9:4.41	The path made by them would be hard to travel again, by those hastening with great speed from here to the good goal.
mahabharata:9:4.42	Remembering what was done by the brave who were slain for my sake, I am discharging that debt and do not set my mind on the kingdom.
mahabharata:9:4.43	Having caused my friends, brothers and grandfathers to fall, if I were to protect my own life, the world would surely reproach me.
mahabharata:9:4.44	What kind of kingdom would it be for me, deprived of kinsmen, companions and friends and bowing to the Pandava?
mahabharata:9:4.45	Having brought such defeat on this world, I shall attain heaven by good fighting; not otherwise.
Thus spoken by Duryodhana, all the kshatriyas honoured his words and said to the king, "Well said, well said."
Not grieving over defeat, with minds fixed on valour, all firmly resolved to fight, they became high-spirited.
Then, having refreshed their mounts, all delighting in battle, the Kauravas went two yojanas less and halted.
In the holy pure sky-like coral, on the auspicious slope of the Himalaya, they reached the red Sarasvati, drank and bathed in its waters.
Your sons, their spirits raised, turned back; then, steadying themselves with one another, all the kshatriyas, O king, urged by time, returned.
Shalya, Chitrasena, the great chariot-warrior Shakuni, Ashvatthaman, Kripa and Kritavarman the Satvata,
Sushena, Arishtasena, the valiant Dhritasena and King Jayatsena—those spent the night there.
With the hero Karna slain in the battle, terrified by the victorious, your sons found no peace except on the Himalaya, the mountain.
They, gathered together there in the presence of the army, striving in battle, honoured the king duly and said:
Make one a leader of the army and then you should fight the enemy; guarded by him, we shall conquer in battle.
Then Duryodhana, standing in the battle, looked at the best of chariot-warriors, knower of all divisions of war, like Death in battle,
fine-limbed, with covered head, conch-necked, sweet-spoken, with lotus-like face, tiger-mouthed, heavy as Meru,
like Sthanu's bull in shoulders, eyes, gait and voice, with long plump arms and broad dense chest,
like the moon in beauty, form and sovereignty of face, with compact joints like masses of gold stone,
with fine round thighs, waist and shins, fine feet, fingers and nails, shaped with effort by the Creator, remembering again and again his virtues,
endowed with every mark, skilled, an ocean of Vedic learning, conqueror of enemies by force, unconquerable by foes,
who knows truly the ten-limbed four-quartered science of the bow, and the four Vedas with their limbs, the legends as fifth,
greatly ascetic, having worshipped the three-eyed one with fierce vows with effort, born of a womb-less mother from Drona the womb-less—
to him, of incomparable deeds, unequalled in form on earth, master of all sciences, ocean of virtues, blameless, Ashvatthaman, your son came and said:
Putting whom before us we may conquer the Pandavas in battle, the preceptor's son is the supreme refuge of all of us today; therefore by your command let him be my commander.
[Drona's son said:] "Shalya, endowed with all virtues—family, valour, splendour, fame and fortune—let him be our commander.
Leaving his own sister's sons, the grateful one has come to us, mighty-armed, like another Mahasena.
Having made him commander, O king, best of kings, we can win victory, like the gods with Skanda, unconquered."
When Drona's son had said this, all the lords of men stood surrounding Shalya and raised cries of victory, set their minds on battle and attained supreme eagerness.
Then Duryodhana, standing on the ground, with joined palms, said to Shalya standing in his chariot, equal to Rama and Bhishma in battle:

This time has come, O friend-loving to friends, when wise men test friend or foe.
mahabharata:9:5.24	So be our hero and leader at the head of the host; when you go to battle the Pandavas will be dull-minded, the Panchalas with their ministers inactive.
[Shalya said:] "O king, Kuru lord, whatever you think of me, I shall do; for your pleasure all my life, kingdom and wealth are yours."
[Duryodhana said:] "I choose you, uncle, incomparable, as commander; protect us, best of warriors, as Skanda the gods in battle.
Be consecrated, O king of kings, as Skanda was by the gods; slay the foes in battle, hero, as Mahendra the danavas."
[Shalya said:] "Duryodhana, mighty-armed, best of speakers, hear: these two Krishnas whom you regard as the best chariot-warriors on a chariot are in no way my equal in strength of arms.
I could fight, enraged, at the head of the battle the whole earth raised against me with gods, asuras and men; what then the Pandavas? I shall conquer in battle the Parthas and the assembled Somakas.
I shall be your leader of the army, no doubt, and I shall make an array that the enemy cannot cross; I tell you this truly, Duryodhana, without doubt."
Thus addressed, the king consecrated the lord of the Madras forthwith in the midst of the army, O best of the Bharatas, with the rite seen in the scriptures, delighted, O lord of men.
When he was consecrated, a great lion-roar arose, and instruments were played in your armies, O Bharata.
The warriors were glad then, and the Madraka great chariot-warriors praised King Shalya, ornament of battle.

Victory, king! Live long, slay the assembled foes. Having obtained the strength of your arms, may Dhritarashtra's mighty sons rule the whole earth with their foes slain.
mahabharata:9:6.9	You are able to conquer in battle gods, asuras and men; what then these mortal Somakas and Srinjayas?
Thus praised, the mighty lord of the Madras, the hero, felt a joy hard to find for the unrestrained.
[Shalya said:] "Today I shall slay in battle all the Panchalas with the Pandavas, king of kings, or slain I shall go to heaven.
Today let the world see me ranging fearless; today let all the sons of Pandu, Vasudeva with Satyaki,
the Panchalas, the Chedis and all the sons of Draupadi, Dhrishtadyumna, Shikhandin and all the Prabhadrakas
see my valour, the great strength of my bow, my dexterity, the power of my weapons and the strength of my arms in the battle.
Today let the Parthas and the siddhas with charanas see what strength I have in my arms and what skill in weapons.
Seeing my valour today, let the great chariot-warriors of the Pandavas turn to retaliation and attempt various deeds.
Today I shall rout the Pandavas' armies on every side, surpassing Drona, Bhishma and the charioteer's son in battle, lord; I shall range in battle fighting for your pleasure, Kaurava."
[Sanjaya said:] When Shalya was consecrated, giver of honour, your armies thought nothing of Karna's calamity, O Bharata.
The soldiers there became glad and cheerful, and thought the Parthas as good as slain, come under the power of the king of the Madras.
Your army, having attained great joy, O best of the Bharatas, slept that night happily, as if in good spirits.
Hearing that sound of your army, King Yudhishthira said to the Varshneya, in the hearing of all kshatriyas:

Shalya, king of the Madras, has been made commander by Dhritarashtra's son, Madhava, the mighty archer honoured among all armies.
mahabharata:9:6.23	Hearing this as it is, do what is fitting, Madhava; you are our leader and protector; ordain what comes next.
Vasudeva said to him, O great king, lord of men: "I know Artayani (Shalya) truly, O Bharata.
He is valiant, of great splendour, and especially great-souled, skilled, a varied fighter, well-equipped, and dexterous.
Such as Bhishma was and Drona and Karna in battle, such or more distinguished I regard the king of the Madras.
Thinking of him fighting in the battle, O Bharata, I find no warrior equal in form, lord of men.
Of Shikhandin, Arjuna, Bhima, the Satvata and Dhrishtadyumna, he is superior in strength in the battle.
The king of the Madras, O great king, with the valour of a lion or an elephant, will range fearless in due time, like Time enraged among creatures.
I see no one to oppose him in the battle today except you, tiger among men, equal in valour to a tiger.
In this whole world with its gods there is no other man than you, Kuru joy, who could slay the king of the Madras enraged in battle, who day after day fighting agitates your army.
So slay Shalya in the battle as Maghavan Shambara; afterwards, that hero is honoured by Dhritarashtra's son.
For you surely is victory when the lord of the Madras is slain in battle; when he is slain the whole great army of Dhritarashtra's son is slain.
Hearing this word of mine now, O great king, go against the mighty king of the Madras in battle, Partha, and slay him, mighty-armed, as Vasava Namuchi.
And do not show pity here, thinking 'He is my mother's brother'; putting kshatriya duty first, slay the lord of the Madras.
Having crossed the ocean of Bhishma and Drona and the netherworld of Karna, do not sink with your host in Shalya, a cow's hoofprint.
Show in the battle your austere power and your kshatriya strength, all of it, and slay this great chariot-warrior."
Having said so much, Keshava, slayer of heroes, went to the camp in the evening, honoured by the Pandavas.
When Keshava had gone, the king of dharma Yudhishthira dismissed all his brothers, the Panchalas and Somakas, and slept that night like an elephant with its thorn removed.
And all those mighty archers, the Panchalas and Pandavas, delighted at Karna's slaying, slept that night.

With the fever gone, the great archer, the great chariot-warrior having crossed to the farther shore, the Pandava army was very glad that night, having won victory by the charioteer's son's slaying, O revered one.
Knowing the king's mind, that army armed itself; they quickly yoked chariots and others ran about.
Elephants were made ready, foot-soldiers armed, and others thousands outfitted horses with coverings.
The sound of instruments arose, O lord of men, to rouse the warriors and the armies.
Then all the forces, the remnant of the army, were seen armed, having made death their return, O Bharata.
Having made Shalya, king of the Madras, commander, the great chariot-warriors, dividing the whole force, stood in the divisions.
Then all your soldiers gathered with your son: Kripa, Kritavarman, Drona's son, Shalya and Shakuni.
And the other remaining kings made a compact then: "None of us is to fight the Pandavas alone in any way.
Whoever fights the Pandavas alone, or abandons one fighting, shall be joined with the five mortal sins and the minor sins; we must fight together, guarding one another."
Having made such a compact, all those great chariot-warriors, putting the king of the Madras first, quickly rushed at the enemy.
Likewise the Pandavas, O king, arraying their army in the great battle, advanced against all the Kauravas, eager to fight on every side.
That force, O best of the Bharatas, roared like an agitated ocean, in the form of a raised ocean with raised chariots and elephants.
[Dhritarashtra said:] "I have heard of the felling of Drona, Bhishma and Radheya; tell me again of Shalya and of my son.
How was Shalya slain in the battle by the king of dharma, Sanjaya, and the mighty-armed Duryodhana, my son, by Bhima?"
[Sanjaya said:] Hear, O king, steadily, as I tell the battle, the destruction of human bodies and of chariots, elephants and horses.
A strong hope arose in your sons then, O king: "With Bhishma, Drona and the charioteer's son felled, Shalya will slay all the Parthas in battle."
Holding that hope in his heart and comforting himself, relying on the king of the Madras, the great chariot-warrior, your son thought himself with a protector.
When Karna was slain and the Parthas raised a lion-roar, then, O king, a great fear came upon Dhritarashtra's sons.
The glorious king of the Madras then comforted them and arrayed an array, O great king, the Sarvatobhadra, prosperous.
The glorious king of the Madras advanced in the battle against the Parthas, shaking his variegated bow, burden-bearing, swifter.
Mounting his excellent chariot with Sindhu horses, the great chariot-warrior, his pennant, O great king, adorned the chariot on which he stood.
Surrounded by that chariot, the hero, tormentor of foes, stood, O great king, dispelling the fear of your sons.
On the march the king of the Madras, armoured, was the mouth of the array, with Madrakas, heroes, and Karna's invincible sons.
On the left was Kritavarman surrounded by Trigartas; Gautama (Kripa) on the right wing with Shakas and Yavanas.
Ashvatthaman was behind, surrounded by Kambojas; Duryodhana was in the middle, guarded by Kuru heroes.
Subala's son too, surrounded by a great horse-force, and the great chariot-warrior Kaitavya went with the whole army.
The mighty-bowed Pandavas, tamers of foes, arraying their army, O great king, in three divisions attacked your army.
Dhrishtadyumna, Shikhandin and the great chariot-warrior Satyaki quickly rushed at Shalya's force in the battle.
Then King Yudhishthira, surrounded by his own army, rushed at Shalya, O best of the Bharatas, wishing to kill him.
Arjuna, destroyer of throngs of foes, swiftly rushed at the mighty archer Hardikya and at the Samshaptaka bands.
Bhimasena at Gautama, and the Somakas, great chariot-warriors, O king of kings, rushed at the enemy in the battle, wishing to kill.
The two sons of Madri, great chariot-warriors with their armies, attacked Shakuni and Uluka in the battle, each with his division.
Likewise your warriors by thousands rushed at the Pandavas in the battle, enraged, with weapons of many kinds in hand.
[Dhritarashtra said:] "With Bhishma, the mighty archer, Drona and Karna the great chariot-warrior slain, and a few of the Kurus left, and the Pandavas still alive in the battle,
the Parthas very enraged and valiant, Sanjaya, what force remained of mine and of the enemy?"
[Sanjaya said:] As we and the enemy stood ready for battle, O king, hear from me what force remained in the battle.
Eleven thousand chariots, O best of the Bharatas, ten thousand and seven hundred elephants,
two hundred thousand horses, O best of the Bharatas, and three crores of men—this was your force.
Six thousand chariots, six thousand elephants, ten thousand horses and one crore foot-soldiers, O Bharata—
this was the Pandavas' force that remained in the battle; only these assembled for battle, O best of the Bharatas.
Thus, dividing, standing by the decision of the king of the Madras, we advanced against the Pandavas, eager for victory, in great fury.
So too the Pandava heroes, victorious in battle, advanced, tigers among men, and the glorious Panchalas.
Thus with floods of troops, each wishing the other's death, the tigers among men advanced at the morning twilight, O lord.
Then began a dreadful, terrible battle between yours and the enemy as they struck one another.
Men, chariots, masses of elephants, horsemen by thousands and valiant horses came together.
The great roar of the fleeing terrible elephants was heard like that of clouds in the sky in due season.
Some chariot-warriors, struck by elephants, fell with their chariots, and heroes fled in the battle, driven by rutting elephants.
The trained chariot-warriors there sent masses of horses and foot-guards to the next world with arrows, O Bharata.
In that dreadful beginning of the night, filled with sorrow and grief, Kritavarman, Kripa and Drona's son sat down together.
From the start a man should act in a way that is fitting, so that he is not joined afterwards with remorse for a thing past.
I cannot abandon King Duryodhana in the battle; it would be ignoble, cruel and ungrateful of me.
[Bhishma said:] "Though urged repeatedly, the noble Gautami did not set her mind on sin against the serpent because of the hunter."
Abandon grief, great king, for it had to be so; you cannot see them again; they were slain in this battle.
This king is to be honoured by me and by you; whoever stays under Dhritarashtra's direction is my friend, and one who is contrary is my enemy and to be put away.
Then, from fear of the king, all the men made a rule, understanding the command of that great-souled king.
Yudhishthira went first, Bhima after him, then Arjuna, and the twins in order.
If they have attained these worlds, those great chariot-warriors, know me, gods, as standing together with those great souls.
